A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same research work, renamed from SciNetBench to SciNet. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite expanded coverage and substantial reformatting.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original evaluations of eight retrieval systems. Section 6 also reports automatic and human evaluations of literature reviews across 20 queries.

after.justification: Tables 1–4 report retrieval and literature-review evaluations, including 40 downstream queries. Section 4.1 and Appendix B additionally report sentiment-label validation and retrieval case studies.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 revises the reported path-construction procedure: v1 selects the maximum-cumulative-citation BFS path as ground truth; v2 treats it as a candidate and applies expert coherence filtering before finalization. The retrieval systems and core scientometric components remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from an AI corpus of approximately 18.6 million papers across 177 subfields to a reported 269-million-paper corpus covering 2,640 subfields in biology, medicine, chemistry, physics, materials science, geology, and AI. The three relational task categories are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 retain the same eight retrieval systems, and Section 6 retains the same four survey-generation conditions. Appendix B presents cases involving existing model families. The new Table 5 compares benchmark designs rather than adding evaluated retrieval baselines.

E3.justification: Reported query counts increase from 354/600/133 to 2,640/4,200/2,100 for ego-centric, pair-wise, and path-wise tasks, while downstream survey evaluation expands from 20 to 40 queries. V2 also reports expert filtering of candidate paths, a new 200-context annotation-validation protocol, and a top-five DPO retrieval case. Core metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a human validation study of GPT-5 citation-sentiment labels and two detailed failure analyses: disruptive-paper retrieval in DPO and reconstruction of the Neocognitron-to-Swin Transformer trajectory. Appendix B and Tables 7–8 provide model outputs and error analyses absent from v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new human–GPT-5 agreement percentage is an annotation-validation result, without accompanying uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 update results throughout: best novelty/disruption recall changes from 1.42%/4.60% to 1.47%/4.71%. Survey results are replaced for the larger sample, and the reported review-quality benefit changes from 23.4% to 25.3%. V2 adds 98% sentiment agreement and case-study outputs. Changed coverage and sample sizes prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The novelty Z-score and tenth-percentile definition, disruption formula, and citation-weighted BFS rationale are retained. The added disruption illustration and construction discussion introduce no new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from an AI-specific retrieval benchmark to a multidisciplinary dataset with 8,940 tasks and a much broader corpus. The three-level taxonomy and claim that existing retrieval systems struggle remain. The abstract also updates the claimed downstream benefit from 23.4% to 25.3%.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.4 discusses citation prestige bias, parsing noise, influence without explicit citations, and limited query diversity. Section 5.2 more explicitly distinguishes plausible narratives from connected citation chains, while Appendix B introduces explanations involving recency bias, semantic drift, and omitted structural milestones.

D1.justification: V2 adds SQLite indexing and 24-core CPU deployment information plus a structured curation and quality-assurance description. The release link changes from an anonymous site to a named GitHub repository, and the subfield inventory is referred there instead of reproduced. Existing Faiss parameters, A100 configuration, and substantive prompt content remain.

R1.justification: Appendix A.1 and Table 5 extend comparisons with LitSearch, PASA, and STARK to corpus scale and supervision signals. V2 adds citation-context and science-mapping references and removes several Shao/Xu references. The central positioning around scholarly relations beyond semantic or entity-based retrieval remains.

P1.justification: V2 retitles and renames the work, revises the abstract and introduction, and polishes terminology and grammar. Appendices are regrouped into supplementary details, case studies, and prompts. The main eight-section sequence and much of the technical exposition remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column ICLR layout to a two-column ICML layout, with extensive figure and table resizing and relocation. V2 adds Figure 3 and Tables 5–8, and redesigns the survey chart with percentage annotations and a Relation-Augmented legend.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens benchmark credibility through the 200-context sentiment validation, explicit expert checking of candidate paths, and substantive limitations discussion. Broader disciplinary evaluation and concrete failure cases also improve applicability and interpretation. These gains outweigh documentation weaknesses, including Figure 5 retaining 133 queries despite the text reporting 2,100. The downstream benefit remains based on providing ground-truth paths, so it does not establish an equivalent gain from a deployed retrieval system.
